18. The learned counsel by referring to the assertion taken in its Affidavit-in-Opposition also contends that, under the provision of section 27kaka(2) of the Act of 1991 this respondent can only send the name of the defaulting-borrower to the banking company and financial institution of the country forwarded by the creditor-banks to it under section 27kaka (1) of the said Act and in the instance case, by publishing the name of the petitioners, this respondent has just complied with the said provision of law, so there is no illegality in publishing the name of the petitioners in the CIB report. 

 20. In contrast, Mr. Khan Mohammad Shameem Aziz, the learned counsel along with Mr. Abu Jafar Mohammad Saleh entered appearance for the respondent No. 4 and also filed Affidavit-in-Opposition and Supplementary-Affidavit denying the material statements so made in the writ petition. By substantiating the averments so taken in the Affidavit-in-Opposition and that of Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition, the learned counsel then contends that, the petitioners took loan from this respondent No. 4 and since the said loan went outstanding, it then filed a Money Suit being Money Suit No. 53 of 1998 and it was decreed on 25-7-1999 and therefore, it filed a Money Execution Case being No. 12 of 2000 which was subsequently renumbered as Artha Jari Case No. 601 of 2003. In course of the said execution case, this respondent obtained a certificate under section 33(5) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 having no scope to say that they are not the defaulting-borrowers. 

 21. The learned counsel further submits that, since one of the scheduled property mortgaged with this respondent had also been mortgaged with Rupali Bank Limited, it then as a 3rd party filed a case being Miscellaneous Case No. 34 of 2004 in its Artha Jari Case No. 601 of 2003 seeking release of the schedule 'Kha' property and the same was released in favour of Rupali Bank Limited. 

 57. In this posture, we find the decision cited by the learned counsel for the petitioners reported in 52 DLR T in particular what has been held in paragraph 8 thereof is squarely applicable given the facts and circumstances of the case rather it would not be out of place to add that the instance case is more forceful than that of cited decision as it is based on the order of this court. Invariably, it is not the true import of section 5gaga or 27kaka to put a company sick for time immemorial on the plea of defaulting-borrower when its earlier liability is being effectively dealt with in the court of law having sufficient security. Further, the main objective of staying the winding up proceeding was to rescue the company from the debt burden and to rebound the company. But the action taken by the creditors has totally jeopardized all its honest effort. If such a hostile attitude continues by the creditor bank towards the promising industry very industrialization in our country would become a far cry. 

 64. From the Affidavit-in-Opposition and Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition filed by respondent No. 4, we find that, it filed a money suit being Money Suit No. 53 of 1998 and upon a decree, it then initiated Money Decree Case No. 12 of 2000 which then re-numbered as Artha Execution Case No. 601 of 2003 which is now pending. By annexing a letter dated 4-12-2016 issued by petitioner No. 2 (Annexure-'VI' to the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition filed by respondent No. 4), it asserted that, the petitioner No. 2 admitted the claim of respondent No. 4 of the loan of 31,00,000 and prayed for providing petitioner No. 1 installment to pay it off and even the petitioner No. 2 gave a cheque amounting to Taka 1,00,000 to respondent No. 4 (though it is dated 4-6-2017). 

 65. It is admitted position, this respondent did not turn up to claim such liability in the winding up proceedings. Then in the agreement dated 17-7-2004 annexed with the application for stay of the winding up proceeding, it was agreed by the earlier management that the liability of this respondent would be paid off by them. Most importantly, the petitioner No. 2 is not any party to the suit or execution case. Also, from Annexure- 'V' and 1/-1' to the Supplementary Affidavit-in-Opposition filed by respondent No. 4, it shows that, earlier management to petitioner No. 1, company failed to live-up their commitment. Had it been the case, then consequence will follow the creditor would realize the default amount though filing case and then through execution case which it has done and the said loan is secured one from where one Rupali Bank liquidated their claim by selling 'kha' scheduled property out of three schedules appended in the schedule of the execution case filed by this respondent No. 4. 

 68. Now let us examine the case of respondent No. 5. 

 74. In any case, this court in the decision reported in 52 DLR 1 also as set at rest the said point asserting that, the borrower who takes over the management unencumbered can in no way be responsible of the previous liabilities which must be vested upon the previous management. The case in hand, the petitioner No. 1, company did not avail any loan after the new management took over the charge of it so, as per the agreement and that of the order of this court staying the winding-up proceeding thus they cannot be treated as defaulting-borrowers.
